https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/01/poli.text: Menü Kereső Magyar Péter 21 EU-s állam vezetőjével együtt közös levélben bírálta Pedro Sánchez migrációs politikáját Külföld Dévai László Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Huszonkét európai uniós tagállam vezetője – köztük Magyarországé is – közös levélben bírálta Pedro Sánchez spanyol miniszterelnök migrációs politikáját, miután az elmúlt napokban mintegy 50 ezer ember érkezett Marokkóból a spanyol fennhatóság alatt álló észak-afrikai Ceutába, a híradások szerint az incidens során legalább 57 ember meghalt. Azóta az enklávét lerohanó több tízezer migráns többsége visszatért Marokkóba. A Politico szerint a levél aláírói úgy vélik, hogy a spanyol kormány intézkedései gyengítik az EU külső határainak védelmét. A levél szerint a vezetők különösen azt kifogásolják, hogy Madrid akár 1,2 millió jogellenesen az országban tartózkodó bevándorló helyzetét is rendezheti. Álláspontjuk szerint egy ilyen nagyszabású legalizáció ösztönzőleg hathat az illegális migrációra, ezért uniós szinten összehangolt fellépést sürgetnek a külső határok megerősítésére és az úgynevezett „vonzó tényezők” megszüntetésére. A spanyol kormány visszautasította a kritikákat. Madrid szerint a Ceutába érkezett migránsok egyike sem lenne jogosult a legalizációs programra, mivel annak szigorú feltételei vannak: csak azok jelentkezhetnek, akik 2026. január 1-je előtt már Spanyolországban éltek, és a kérelem benyújtásakor legalább öt hónapja folyamatosan ott tartózkodtak. A spanyol külügyminisztérium hangsúlyozta azt is, hogy a jelentkezési határidő már júniusban lejárt. A 22 ország vezetője ugyanakkor arra figyelmeztetett, hogy nem szabad azt az üzenetet közvetíteni, hogy az illegális belépés később jogszerű tartózkodássá válhat. A levélben azt is jelezték, hogy szükség esetén készek ideiglenesen visszaállítani a belső határellenőrzést a schengeni övezetben, és videókonferenciát kezdeményeztek az uniós belügyminiszterek között a további lépések egyeztetésére. Sánchez saját levelében élesen bírálta európai kollégáit. A spanyol miniszterelnök szerint a Spanyolország schengeni tagságának felfüggesztését sürgető javaslatok ellentétesek az európai joggal, a humanitárius elvekkel és az uniós szolidaritással. Úgy fogalmazott, hogy több tagállam előítéletek, álhírek, tudatlanság vagy politikai érdekek alapján reagál a kialakult helyzetre, miközben szerinte az Európai Unió nem engedheti meg magának az ilyen önző, megosztó és jogellenes fellépést. A levéllel kapcsolatban megkerestük a külügyminisztériumot is. Megkeresésünk után Orbán Anita külügyminiszter a Facebook-oldalán közzétett egy bejegyzést, amiben azt írja, Magyar Péter miniszterelnök 21 uniós kollégájával együtt közös levélben bírálta Pedro Sánchez spanyol miniszterelnök migrációs politikáját. Orbán a Ceutában történtekről azt írja, nyugtalanító emlékeket idéz fel 2015-ből, amikor „Európa külső határait gyakorlatilag áttörték”. Szerinte a spanyol Legfelsőbb Bíróság e hónap elején hozott ítélete – amely kimondta, hogy a határt átúszva érkező embereket nem lehet azonnal visszaküldeni – hozzájárulhatott az elmúlt napok migrációs eseményeihez. A miniszter közölte, hogy szombaton folyamatosan egyeztetett külügyminiszter kollégáival az ügyben, mert szerinte azonnali cselekvésre van szükség. A bejegyzésében megismételte azt az álláspontot, amit a levélben is hangsúlyoznak az aláíró államok. Orbán Anita bejegyzését azzal zárta, hogy minden ország, így Spanyolország is felelősséget visel az Európai Unió külső határainak védelméért, és hangsúlyozta, hogy a magyar kormány minden körülmények között kiáll az illegális migrációval szemben, valamint Magyarország határainak védelme mellett. (Frissítés: A cikk címét Orbán Anita bejegyzése után módosítottuk, a szöveget pedig kiegészítettük a külügyminiszter posztjával.) Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! https://www.politico.eu/article/hopes-fo.text: LONDON — Nigel Farage ruled out entering talks with right-wing rival Rupert Lowe Monday — unless Lowe moves to expel a controversial ally. The pathway to power for Farage’s Reform UK was already narrowing before new Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s takeover aided a polling bounce for the governing Labour Party. While still polling in the single digits, Rupert Lowe’s splinter party has been proving it can eat into a significant chunk of Reform’s vote. Lowe formed Restore Britain after being kicked out of Reform — but he has been, at least ostensibly, dangling an olive branch for Farage to grasp in recent weeks. Advertisement Advertisement On Monday the prospect of the two warring factions signing a make-up pact seemed to be at an impasse. Farage used a press conference in Westminster to publicly state a new condition for holding discussions with “that party,” as he referred to Restore. Lowe must, he said, kick out Restore’s co-founder — a move Lowe has already rejected . “I’m always happy to meet people and talk to people — within reason,” Farage said when asked by POLITICO what his conditions for entering talks with Lowe would be. Leader of Restore Britain Rupert Lowe speaks to the media in Wigan, England on June 18, 2026. | Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images “But I do think it’s fair to say that there are one or two people in the orbit of the upper echelons of that party who, if I sat down and talked to, I think our members and our voters would be utterly shocked that I’d done it,” he added. “So we can talk to Rupert Lowe — that’s fine. But when you have co-founders, etcetera, putting out what I would call the ‘old theory’ — the old theory that we probably haven’t heard in this country since 1936 — and you have other adjacent publicly-supportive people demanding that all Jews be removed from the country, just as an example… “So the condition I would put on it is those people would have to be out of the inner circle — and I think that for me would be the only way we could sensibly proceed.” Advertisement Advertisement The co-founder Farage referred to is Charlie Downes, who was this month accused of implying that Farage had been “ bought ” by Jewish supporters. Campaigners against anti-semitism accused Downes of perpetuating the “oldest smear” against Jewish people. Farage’s attack on “publicly-supportive people demanding that all Jews be removed from the country” is meanwhile a reference to Steve Laws, a backer of Restore Britain who is an advocate of “ total remigration .” Lowe told POLITICO in June that Laws plans “no part in our decision-making process,” although Lowe said he is “very welcome” to support the party. Lowe had already indicated his opposition to booting out Downes after the Telegraph first reported Farage’s rejection of talks. “Farage and Reform have also said that Restore Britain must outright sack Charlie Downes — putting a young Christian man out of work, just as he is looking to build his life and start a family,” Lowe wrote on X . “That is simply not how I operate.” While still polling in the single digits, Rupert Lowe’s splinter party has been proving it can eat into a significant chunk of Reform’s vote. | Darren Staples/AFP via Getty Images It’s the latest twist in a convoluted saga that is commanding attention on the right of British politics. Lowe last week offered to put “ past disagreements ” with Farage aside so that the pair can work together. But he set five conditions for doing so, including the exclusion of Conservative defectors to Reform from a future Farage cabinet. Prisons push Farage’s comments came at a press conference he held to add to pressure on the new prime minister over Britain’s prisons, which have in recent years been hovering around breaking point. Advertisement Advertisement Farage said Reform UK will begin talks with El Salvador about renting prison space so a future government he leads could deport all foreign prisoners to serve their sentences abroad — an echo of Donald Trump’s controversial policy for prisoners from the U.S. Other possible countries that could forge similar deals, Farage suggested, are Kosovo, as well as Estonia or Lithuania. Reform claimed the plans would free up 10,000 spaces in U.K. prisons. However, nearly a third of foreign nationals in detention are on remand, meaning they haven’t been convicted of a crime and are awaiting trial. Pressed about the disparity, home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf told POLITICO: “That’s not the gotcha that you might think it is. “The vast majority of those people end up being convicted — so in terms of the practical plan that we’ve laid out, it makes no difference.”

https://www.dw.com/en/can-turkey-s-new-p.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IeBb Although the PKK announced its dissolution a year ago, it remains unclear whether all its fighters will lay down their arms Image: Sterk tv Advertisement One year ago, the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) burned its weapons in a symbolic ceremony. The move was seen as a sign of its willingness to disband. Since then, the Kurdish side has been calling on the Turkish government to take political steps. Now, parliament has passed a bill submitted by the conservative Islamic ruling party AKP and its ultranationalist ally. Officially called the "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration," it is intended to provide the legal framework for the ongoing peace process. According to official figures, 467 out of 592 MPs voted in favor of the bill. The ruling party and its ally see this as the beginning of a new era: Under certain conditions, the bill provides for a suspension of sentences for PKK members — but only after the PKK and its affiliated groups have been confirmed to have disbanded and disarmed, so that peace, brotherhood and solidarity can prevail throughout the entire country. The pro-Kurdish DEM party also supports the bill, but it views it only as a first step that must be followed by further reforms. The pro-Kurdish DEM party also voted in favor of the PKK law. At the same time, it is calling for swift political and legal reforms Image: Adem Altan/AFP PKK law divides society and parliament Fierce opposition came from the ultranationalist opposition party IYI. Even during consultations, its delegate Ayyuce Turkes, daughter of the founder of the ultranationalist and right-wing extremist Grey Wolves, accused the government of rushing a landmark bill through parliament. She also criticized what she felt was an overly conciliatory stance toward PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan. She avoided using his name, calling him a "baby killer" instead, just as government agencies and media have done for decades. There was even a physical altercation. The debate highlights just how deep the divides are within Turkish society. While the ultranationalist IYI party rejects the process, the MHP, from which the Grey Wolves emerged, is now among its most important supporters — even though it had, previously, vehemently opposed earlier peace initiatives. Observers believe this shift in course and the progress in the peace process are also a result of the changed security situation in the region. Among other things, they mention the fall of the Assad regime in Syria , the war in Gaza and the conflict between Israel, the United States and Iran . Syria and Iran are also home to large Kurdish populations that are supported by various regional actors. According to the prevailing view, a more stable relationship with the Kurds who live within Turkey's own borders could provide Ankara with more leeway in domestic and foreign policy. The justice committee of the Turkish parliament convened to discuss the draft "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration" Image: ANKA What's in the law? The law applies to convictions for PKK membership, propaganda, financing or intentional support of the organization and its structures. For prison sentences of up to 15 years, enforcement is to be suspended for five years; for longer or life sentences, the suspension is to last ten years. Ongoing investigations are to be put on hold. According to pro-government media, up to 3,600 prisoners could benefit from this. The prerequisite is the complete disbanding of the PKK and the surrender of all its weapons and ammunition. Both of these conditions have to be verified by Turkish authorities and, subsequently, officially confirmed by the National Security Council, chaired by Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan . Excluded are PKK members who were convicted prior to June 1, 2005 — the date on which the current penal code came into force — as well as those convicted of homicide and whose convictions are final. That means the regulation does not apply to PKK founder Ocalan either. In February 2025, the 77-year-old had called on the PKK to disband, declared an end to the armed struggle and spoke out in favor of a political solution. Turkey: An end to the Kurdish conflict? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video PKK views law as a mere first step The PKK also calls the bill a first step; it criticizes, however, wording and content. Its key demand remained unfulfilled: As long as Ocalan cannot directly coordinate the peace process under conditions of freedom, the issue of disarmament could not be resolved either. They said penal code regulations alone did not go far enough, more comprehensive democratization reforms were needed. The message was that as long as returning fighters or exiled politicians continued to be criminalized and were unable to engage in political activities legally, hardly any of them would leave the mountains where they've been staying. PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan in February 2026. The law passed by Turkey's parliament does not provide for his release from prison Image: DEM Even legal pro-Kurdish political activity has ben restricted in Turkey for decades: parties were banned, politicians were arrested or barred from political activity. To this day, elected mayors are being removed from office, and numerous politicians and activists are in prison. Among them are two former co-chairs of the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP) that mainly represented Kurds, Selahattin Demirtas and Figen Yuksekdag. Peace without democratization? Political scientist Berk Esen criticizes the law for failing to offer concrete democratic solutions to the Kurdish issue. He also noted that, parallel to the peace process involving the PKK, the government had significantly increased the pressure on the largest opposition party CHP. For about two years, the Turkish judiciary has increasingly been cracking down on leading CHP politicians. Critics view this as an attempt to weaken the government party's strongest political rival. Among the most high-profile cases is that of former mayor of Istanbul and CHP presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu . He and hundreds of other party members are in prison, on charges of fraud and corruption. The entire CHP leadership under Ozgur Ozel was removed as well. He formed a new party several weeks ago. Criticism of Erdogan's role Esen primarily criticizes Erdogan's strong influence on the peace process. Although it is to be implemented by a committee chaired by the vice president and key ministers, who are also heads of the intelligence services and the National Security Council, Esen argues that it will ultimately be Erdogan as chairman of the National Security Council who decides when and which steps in the peace process will be implemented. This assessment is also shared by Reha Ruhavioglu, director of the Kurdish Studies Center. "Erdogan will clearly set the pace," Ruhavioglu said, attributing this to the asymmetric balance of power between the Turkish state and the PKK. In addition, Erdogan had learned his lessons from the failure of the peace talks between 2013 and 2015 and would now certainly assemble more control in his own hands. At the same time, experts say, Erdogan has his sights set firmly on the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections, and would want to limit any political risks associated with the process. Ruhavioglu expects further controversy, especially if former PKK fighters return to Turkey and remain at large. The government is therefore likely to allow their return, suspended sentences and political activity only gradually, and largely in response to public reaction. This article was originally written in German. Photo by Russia President Office/UPI Sept. 12 (UPI) -- President Vladimir Putin on Friday warned European countries that sending troops into Ukraine would mean "war with Russia." Putin was speaking to reporters at the BRICS summit in New Delhi when he issued his stark warning. "Now, they say they are thinking of how to deploy troops to Ukraine," he told reporters, as quoted by state-run news agency TASS . "This would mean a war with Russia." Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Last week, French President Emmanuel Macron said 26 countries had pledged to support sending troops to Ukraine in a peacekeeping mission to provide postwar guarantees. "The day the conflict stops, the security guarantees will be deployed," Macron told reporters . On Saturday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov reiterated the Russian president's position. "It's not a red line, but Russia's position that has been conveyed to the whole world, primarily to Europeans, in an extremely specific and clear manner," Peskov told reporters . Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the country had been hit by nearly 500 attack drones throughout Saturday. Advertisement Advertisement "The Russians are burning warehouses with food and gas stations, pharmaceutical facilities and ordinary passenger trains, residential buildings and civilian businesses," Zelensky said in a statement on X . "Just in the past few days, they have struck a steel plant owned by an Indian business, an American company that produced sunflower oil, and a Polish company that manufactured plumbing fixtures. "Russian attacks have targeted truck parking lots, ports, shopping malls, and energy infrastructure." On Friday, jet-powered Russian drones struck several gas stations in Kyiv. Two people were killed and 12 injured. "This is probably one of the most difficult periods of the war because life is just like on a rollercoaster," Anastasiia Demchenko, who works near one of the gas stations, told the Guardian . "It feels like life is on the edge." Russia has recently increased attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Ukraine has struck Russian oil facilities on the port city of Makhachkala, on the Caspian Sea. Photograph: George Chan/AAP Sydney Teens at Sydney private religious school made to share beds with teachers, inquiry hears Former student says nothing untoward happened to her during stays but tells NSW parliamentary inquiry culture of Redeemer Baptist School left much to ‘untangle’ as an adult Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian Associated Press Mon 12 Oct 2026 02.50 EDT Last modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 03.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Teens at a private religious school were made to share beds with teachers, while its principal once wandered through a common area naked, former students claim. A NSW parliamentary inquiry on Monday was told of the disturbing allegations from two former students of western Sydney’s Redeemer Baptist School. Edward Garth, 23, said he was shunned after “escaping” the broader Redeemer community in November. He told the committee about a study-stay during school holidays when he slept in the same building as principal and church elder Jonathon Cannon. “I remember one night before dinner, I was in the kitchen getting a drink,” Garth said. “As I walked into the living room, which was my bedroom at the time, I saw [Cannon], my principal, walk out of the bathroom into the living room naked before heading to his room. “He was startled, and when they saw me, he ran to his room. I don’t know why he didn’t cover himself with a towel.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Garth said he reported the incident, but it got back to Cannon, the principal’s brother Noel and the then-pupil’s own parents, who scolded him. Former student Emma Hughes told the inquiry the culture inside the school left much for students to “untangle” as adults. School camps, away from parents, were especially anxiety-inducing. On occasion, a student would have to share a bed with teachers in a caravan park or school-owned cabins to save space, she said. Her submission stated nothing untoward happened to her during the stays. “Usually, the student would be a community member, which in itself says they knew maybe they shouldn’t be doing it,” she said. “But I recall when I was in year 6, I would share a bed with [a] teacher, and in an effort to be fair, she made it so we would rotate every night … so that we all didn’t have to.” Staff, often known by kinship titles like “uncle”, regularly crossed conversational boundaries, Hughes said. “Often, personal things were discussed in very public matters,” she said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “The nature of boundaries is really something which is not particularly, I believe, understood by staff at Redeemer in the way we understand it in most school contexts.” The school also had an emphasis on surveillance and “dobbing”, public humiliations and punishment, she said. A boy and girl were made to stand on chairs in front of a year 7 class after teachers intercepted a love note, Hughes said of her time at the school. Noel Cannon read the note to a collection of students before they were “dressed-down in front of four year groups and many teachers”, she said. The parliamentary committee is investigating the management of the Parramatta-based school and oversight from government bodies. The Communities and Justice Department received 15 risks of significant harm notifications since 2004 but they had not triggered a field assessment, an earlier response to questions on notice revealed. Cannon and other school representatives were invited to appear at the inquiry and state the school’s case. Committee chair Abigail Boyd said she was disappointed an attempted summons to appear went begging. AAP has contacted the school for comment on the students’ allegations.
